citation: The Chicago Democrat. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, 1833-1835. Seventy-three issues, Vol. I No. 1 (Tuesday, November 26, 1833) through Vol. II No. 18 (Wednesday, August 26, 1835), in OCR-assisted research transcription.
author: John Calhoun, editor and publisher
repository: Page scans of bound volumes supplied to this project by the project owner; the transcriptions of them are the owner's own work product, made to the method in chicago/reference/newspapers/Transcriptions/Newspaper_Transcription_Workflow.md. The 1833 first issue additionally carries a Chicago Historical Society ownership stamp and the pencilled number 51177.
locator: By issue date, then issue page and column, as set out under the citation convention in the note. The per-issue index is chicago/4d/data/research/newspapers/corpus.json.
note:
THE TOWN'S OWN NEWSPAPER, ACROSS THE WHOLE OF THE PERIOD THIS PROJECT RECONSTRUCTS. The Democrat was Chicago's first newspaper and for eighteen months its only one; the scene date, 1835-07-01, is a Wednesday on which an issue was printed. Seventy-three issues are transcribed here, from the first to 1835-08-26. What the single 1833-11-26 issue already gave this dataset — trades being carried on, self-reported addresses, the village ordinances, arrivals and clearances, a population figure — this run gives eighty more times over, and across the twenty months in which the town went from about eight hundred people to three thousand two hundred.

THE PER-ISSUE RECORD FOR 1833-11-26 STAYS, AND IT OUTRANKS THIS ONE FOR THAT ISSUE. data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json was made by reading the page scans directly at 2.4x-9x, and it is senior to any transcription-mediated reading of the same paper. It also holds the corrections and negative findings that only a scan read produces, and this record does not restate or replace them.

RULING 2 OF T-0256, VERBATIM, AND IT GOVERNS EVERY CLAIM TAKEN FROM THIS RUN: “Transcription-mediated readings grade `documented`, carrying a flag. The corpus is read through OCR-assisted transcriptions, not the page scans. Every claim taken this way carries `reading: transcription_mediated` and preserves the transcription's own uncertainty brackets. This EXTENDS, and does not overturn, data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json's standard — where a scan exists and is read, the scan remains the authority (it caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'), and a transcription-mediated claim upgrades when a scan read confirms it.”

THE TRAPS ARE CORPUS-WIDE, AND THEY ARE THE 1833-11-26 RECORD'S OWN, RESTATED BECAUSE THEY DO NOT STOP AT ONE ISSUE.

1. A STOCK CUT IS NOT A PICTURE OF A CHICAGO BUILDING. Nineteenth-century jobbing printers kept generic engravings for property, estray, runaway and shipping notices, and the same block was struck for any advertisement in the category. No elevation, storey count, window arrangement, roof form or vessel rig may be taken from one. The transcriptions render these as bracketed descriptions of a cut; a bracketed description of an engraving is not evidence of a building.

2. AN ADVERTISEMENT'S OWN DATE IS THE DATE OF THE COPY, NOT OF THE ISSUE. Standing matter ran for weeks and months. 'Nov. 22, 1833' at the foot of a column in a February 1834 paper dates the writing of the advertisement; it says the trade was being carried on in November, and it says the advertiser had not cancelled by February. Both readings are worth having and they are different readings.

3. A LATER HAND IS NOT LETTERPRESS. The 1833-11-26 scan carries a pencilled 'S. W.' in the right margin, in a later hand, positioned so that transcribing it would look like contemporary corroboration of a corner the type does not name. Anything not printed — pencil, stamp, accession number, marginal note — is quarantined wherever it appears in this run.

4. A PRINTED NUMBER THAT REPEATS IS PRESERVED, NOT REPAIRED. The Democrat prints Vol. II No. 5 twice (1835-01-21 and 1835-05-20) and Vol. II No. 18 twice (1835-08-19 and 1835-08-26); the American prints Vol. I No. 12 twice (1835-08-22 and 1835-08-29). The transcriptions preserve the printed number and say so. Cite the DATE; the volume and number are what the masthead claims, not an index.

5. AN OCR-ASSISTED READING IS NOT A DIPLOMATIC EDITION. The corpus's own workflow document says so in its release standard: 'Call the result a high-accuracy, OCR-assisted research transcription, not a fully diplomatic edition, unless every line has received human visual verification. Before quoting a bracketed passage in publication, return to the cited source page and column.' Degraded columns in this run are visibly degraded — whole passages of recognition debris survive in the text — and a name read out of one is a candidate, not a citizen.

HOW TO CITE ONE ISSUE. Publication, issue date, Vol./No. as printed, the issue page and column from the transcription's own markers, then the text file and the line range. A claim that cannot name its column cannot be made. The markers come in five dialects across this deposit — T-0256 quotes one of them as though it were universal and it covers 49 of the 86 issues — and every one of the five carries a page and a column: `===== ISSUE PAGE n / [SOURCE ]PDF PAGE m / COLUMN k OF j =====`; a `Newspaper Page n — Source PDF Page m` heading followed by `Column k`; a `SOURCE PDF PAGE n` banner followed by `--- Column k ---`; `[Source PDF page m; newspaper page n; column k]`; and `--- SOURCE PDF PAGE m, COLUMN k ---`. data/research/newspapers/corpus.json records which dialect each issue uses, the text a citation resolves against, its sha256 and its page and column counts; tools/check_newspaper_corpus.py holds all of that every commit.

WHERE THE TEXT IS. chicago/reference/newspapers/Transcriptions/ — the owner's archival deposit, which this project reads and never writes. Sixty-seven issues ship a committed .txt and are cited at their reference path; the rest ship as .docx only and their text is extracted by tools/docx_text.py into chicago/4d/data/research/newspapers/text/, deterministically, brackets and markers intact. Neither reaches the published site: the corpus is research, not payload, and the gate holds that in three places.

A CORRECTION TO THE TICKET THAT COMMISSIONED THIS RECORD, made while building the index and worth more than it looks. T-0256 states that the 1835-07-08 Democrat is partial, its fourth page absent from the source PDF. That was true of the first transcription of it and is no longer true of the deposit: a second, later reading of a COMPLETE four-page scan of the same issue is present, and the corpus cites that one — the partial is kept as an alternate, because two readings of the same issue are worth comparing. The issue a week after the scene date is not short after all. The same preference rule applies wherever an issue is transcribed twice: a complete scan beats a partial one, and at equal completeness the committed .txt — the deliverable the set's own manifest measures — beats the .docx-only reading.
access_notes: Held in the repository and deliberately outside the published payload: 86 issues of transcription is about 11 MB of text, of which 2.7 MB is derived here. The page scans and the source PDFs are local-only (see the repository's .gitignore); the transcriptions are what is committed. Nothing in data/research/ is copied by tools/publish.sh.
what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago on a stated date, weekly, from November 1833 to August 1835
self-reported addresses, at the precision the advertiser chose to give — usually a street or a junction, rarely a corner
the survival or disappearance of a business between two dates, by whether its advertisement is still running
dissolution, removal and replacement notices, which are the only evidence that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town (T-0256 ruling 3)
post-office letter lists, which name residents by the hundred — a listed name alone makes a resident candidate, recorded `letter_list_only: true` (T-0256 ruling 1)
the corporation's ordinances and the notices of its officers
arrivals and clearances at the harbour, with vessel, master and cargo
public sales, auctions, and the notices of the canal and harbour works
the paper's own imprint, week by week — self-reported, and therefore about as good as an address gets
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's dimensions, form, material, storey count or fenestration
the specific corner of any junction it names, unless the type says which
a picture of any Chicago building — every engraving in the run is a printer's stock cut

a settled date for the three supplied 1833 scan pages: the filename says 11-16, the 'Verified' reading's own text reports NOV. 19, 1833 at the top of supplied page 1, and the scan-read record dates the set 1833-11-26
a diplomatic text — every reading here is OCR-assisted, and a bracketed passage must be checked against the scan before it is quoted
evidence that a building named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01, which is a survival liberty and is stated on the record that takes it
